Devlog: November 2026

32 updates to Tailwinds in November 2026, newest first. The devlog index lists every month.

November 12, 2026

Sandbox games: choose your starting money

A new game can now be a Sandbox, for trying out aircraft, marketing, loyalty and hubs without having to save up for them first. Switch it on on the Launch step of a new game.

  • Choose your starting money: $10M, $50M, $250M or $1B, or type any amount from $1M to $10B. In a game that starts in a historical year, the amount is scaled to that year’s money, as the usual $10M is.
  • Instant deliveries, if you want them: aircraft arrive the moment you sign, paid in full, with no wait on the factory line, and crew you hire start work straight away, so a new aircraft can fly this week. Launch orders still wait for the type to enter service. Browse what is on offer in the aircraft guide.
  • Board objectives start switched off in a sandbox. You can switch them back on.
  • Everything else is the normal game: rivals, demand, events, costs and bankruptcy are all unchanged.
  • You choose a sandbox when you start a new game, and you can’t switch it on or off later. Sandbox games show a Sandbox badge in the top bar and on their save cards.

November 12, 2026

Banks now ask whether you can pay (new games)

Until now a loan was sized by your revenue or by the aircraft you own, and nothing else. An airline losing money could still borrow sixteen weeks of revenue, and every Aircraft Finance loan bought the planes that secured the next one. In games started from today, lenders also look at what you earn and what you are worth.

  • Earnings. Your loan repayments, including the new loan, may take at most half of your operating cash flow: your weekly profit before loan repayments, averaged over the last four weeks.
  • Debt to equity. Total borrowing may not exceed four times your equity: your cash plus the aircraft you own, less what you already owe.
  • Starting out is unchanged. The $5M, $10M and $20M base loans are always available, so a brand-new airline with no results can still get going.
  • The loan desk says which limit applies, “limited by earnings” or “limited by debt-to-equity”, next to each loan’s available amount.

Games you have already started keep the old rules for good.

November 12, 2026

A Brand page: why travellers pick you

The Reputation tab is now Brand, and it answers the question it always hinted at: when travellers have a choice, do they pick you or a rival, and why?

  • Business and leisure travellers, separately. Each gets a verdict from Weak to Excellent against the average rival on your routes, and the two or three things helping or hurting most, in plain words: “More flights than rivals”, “Fares higher than rivals”, “Brand not well known yet”.
  • They want different things. Leisure travellers weigh price most and are twice as swayed by targeted campaigns. Business travellers weigh quality and frequency, and only they use lounges. So the same airline can be a favourite with one and an also-ran with the other.
  • See all factors lists every factor, how much it shifts the odds, and on how many of your routes you are ahead. These are the same numbers that share out passengers each week, not an estimate.
  • Routes you fly alone are left out of the verdicts, because there is no one to beat. There the same things decide how many people fly at all.
  • Quality gets its own card with what is lifting it and what is holding it back, such as “Too many delays” or “Ageing fleet”.
  • Marketing has moved here from Operations, beside the awareness it buys. Your reputation score and the market positioning map are folded away at the foot of the page.

More on how travellers choose in the route economics guide.

November 11, 2026

Hubs sell the connections that make sense

A focus city with 147 routes was carrying one connecting passenger a week. Three things were wrong with how hubs sold and counted connections. They are fixed in every game, saved ones included.

Read the full update →

November 11, 2026

Route quotes now count connections over routes you have just opened

  • The quote was too low while you were building a hub. In games with connection seats, the Route Planner and Route Finder worked out connecting passengers from last week's flights. A route you had opened since then had no flights to read, so nothing was counted as connecting over it. Open six spokes in one sitting and the seventh was quoted as if the other six were not there. On one test hub a route was quoted $5,400 a week of connecting revenue and then earned $25,000.
  • New routes are now forecast. A route with no week flown yet is forecast at its settled load, the same week the quote itself describes, and connections are seated over it. This matters most in the first week of a new game and whenever you add several routes before advancing the week. Nothing changes in what a route actually earns. See the hub strategy guide for how connecting passengers are seated.

November 11, 2026

Thirteen more aircraft: the non-ER 767s and 777s, two A340s and the Tu-144

A player on Discord, Dunno23, sent a list of real variants the market did not have. They are all in now, in new and existing saves. Era games get each one in its real year.

  • Before the ER. The 767-200 and 767-300, the 777-200 and 777-300, and the DC-10-10 are the first versions of aircraft the game only had in long-range form. They cost less to buy and burn a little less, and they stop at 6,500 to 11,000 km. If your network is domestic or regional you no longer pay for range you never use. The wide-body guide has them side by side.
  • Two more A340s. The A340-200 trades seats for range against the -300 (14,800 km). The A340-500 goes further than any other four-engine jet in the game, 16,670 km, and is one of the most expensive ways to move a passenger that far.
  • Small and long 737s. The 737-600 seats 132 and has the range of the bigger 737NGs. The 737-700ER carries extra tanks in the hold and reaches 10,695 km with a 48-seat premium cabin. Fit all 149 seats and it manages about 7,200 km, so it suits a long thin premium route and little else.
  • The first A320 and A321. The A320-100 and A321-100 came before the extra fuel tanks. They are the cheapest way into each size, with 3,300 km and 4,350 km of range. See the narrow-body guide.
  • 747-400ER. 14,045 km, about 600 km more than the standard -400, for more fuel and a higher price.
  • Tupolev Tu-144. The Soviet supersonic airliner joins Concorde. It charges the same supersonic fares, carries 150, and runs out of fuel at 3,300 km. It will rarely make money. It is on the flagships page.

Rival airlines run by the game do not buy any of the thirteen, so an existing save keeps the competitors it has. Each new type joins the maintenance family of its siblings and has its own shape in the cabin designer.

November 10, 2026

Hub banks: your timetable now decides who connects (new games)

Until today, any two of your flights at a hub connected, whatever time they left, and the game assumed a flat hour and a half between them. In games you start from now on, hubs work the way real ones do.

  • Hubs run on banks. A bank is a wave: flights land close together, passengers change planes, and flights leave close together. Every hub you designate gets them, your Focus Cities included.
  • A connection has to fit the clock. A passenger can connect when the inbound flight lands between 40 minutes and 6 hours before the onward one leaves. The more of your flights that meet, and the shorter the wait, the better the connection sells against a rival’s nonstop. Two spokes your timetable never brings together sell no connecting tickets at all.
  • You don’t have to do anything. The automatic timetable banks every hub for you: three banks a day at a Focus City or Hub, four at a Major Hub, six at an International Gateway. In our test network an airline that never opens the Schedule page ends two years within about 1% of where the old rule would have left it.
  • Aircraft wait for the wave. To come back on a bank, an aircraft sits at the far end for up to four hours, or sleeps there overnight to make the first bank of the morning. That is the price of banking: a busy aircraft fits fewer round trips into its week.
  • A card for every hub on Operations ▸ Schedule shows when flights land and leave through the day, how many connections your timetable makes each week, the average wait and how long your aircraft sit waiting. Pick three, four or six banks, set your own bank times, or go Rolling: no waiting, but passengers only connect where flights happen to meet. The same test network on Rolling ends about 4% poorer.
  • Move a flight off a bank and it is marked on the timeline. Its panel tells you which bank each landing and departure makes and how many flights it meets, and Snap to the bank puts it back. Typed times and dragging work as before; the round trip now includes any wait for a bank.
  • Charters keep the customer’s times. A charter never waits for a bank and no bank setting moves it. Your own flights on that aircraft are banked around it.

Games already in progress keep the old rule and nothing in them changes. To start a new game without banks, untick Hub banks on the setup screen. The hub strategy guide has more on how banks work.

November 10, 2026

Big airlines run faster

  • The Fleet page opens at once. It used to build a row for every aircraft you own, which took half a second at 600 aircraft and two seconds at 1,500. It now builds only the rows on screen and opens in about a tenth of a second at either size.
  • Weeks advance faster on large networks. With 1,500 routes, pressing Next Week froze the page for about five seconds. It is now about a second and a half. At 600 routes it went from 0.9 seconds to 0.6.
  • Fare and schedule changes too. The sums behind every change you make are about a third quicker up to 1,000 routes, and four to five times quicker beyond that, where the game had been repeating work it had already done.
  • None of the game’s numbers changed. Demand, fares and profits come out exactly as before.
  • One thing to know: on fleets of more than 150 aircraft your browser’s find-in-page only sees the rows on screen. Use the search box above the list instead.

These fixes come from Headwinds, where the largest airlines now run to several thousand aircraft.

November 10, 2026

Type your timetable

  • Type a departure time. On Operations ▸ Schedule, click any flight and type when it leaves, as a local time at the airport it leaves from. 07:30, 0730, 19 and 7pm all work, so there is no more clicking +15 minutes over and over.
  • Set a route’s whole week in one go. The same panel shows the route’s week as rows of a time and the days it flies. A route that flies 14 times a week is two times typed once, not fourteen flights moved one by one. Untick days, or add a row, for a flight that only runs on some days.
  • Then change single days. If Saturday’s flight should leave later than the rest, click it and give it a time of its own. The week reads back exactly as you set it.
  • It tells you what is in the way. Two departures closer together than the aircraft’s round trip are refused, with the earliest time that would work. If a time is taken by a flight you set on another route, or by a charter, that day’s flight leaves at the nearest free time and the panel says which one moved.
  • Dragging flights and the nudge buttons work as before. Your timetable still sets the departure board only; it doesn’t change demand or costs.

November 10, 2026

Figures that now match your bill

  • Gate fees by airport. Finance ▸ By Airport priced every gate at the first gate’s rate, so a big hub looked far cheaper, and far more profitable, than it was. It now shows the same gate bill as the P&L.
  • Maintenance on the Fleet page. Every maintenance figure there ignored your maintenance budget and your maintenance team’s pay. Rows, cards and the weekly total now show what you are actually charged, the same as Finance.
  • Fleet utilisation warns you before it hurts. The Dashboard card used to stay green all the way to 100%. It now turns amber past 85%, says when a tight timetable is costing you on-time performance, and in newer games shows the week’s risk of an operational meltdown.
  • The “Fill the aircraft” board mandate measures load factor the way the Dashboard does: passengers over seats, so a big trunk route counts for more than a small spoke.
  • Smaller corrections: hub investment is in the year-to-date G&A total, the airport page no longer says gates get dearer in games where a big tenant gets a discount, and the in-game Help now describes loans and meltdowns as they really work.

November 9, 2026

The Advisor, and a briefing for your own AI

  • A new Advisor page under Company reads your airline and lists what to do about it, most urgent first: aircraft sitting idle (with a button that opens the Route Finder on that type), aircraft with hours to spare, routes that are full but losing money, routes flying mostly empty, routes selling out, heavy checks coming due with nothing booked, gates nearly full, unfunded marketing, unhedged fuel and more. Every tip says why and takes you to the screen that fixes it.
  • It won’t give bad advice on young routes. Routes in their first 16 weeks are left out while demand builds, and if your maintenance team is paid well enough to book its own heavy checks, the Advisor doesn’t nag you to book them.
  • The Dashboard shows one line with the number of suggestions and the top one, so you see it at a glance.
  • Copy airline briefing. One button puts your airline on the clipboard as plain text — cash and recent profit, the Advisor’s tips, your best and worst routes with fares, your fleet, gates and settings. Paste it into Claude, ChatGPT or any AI chat and ask it anything about your airline. Nothing is sent anywhere by the game. See route economics for what the route figures mean.
  • The briefing knows its way around. It now ends with where every page is, in the classic layout and the map view, and each tip names its exact screen (Finance ▸ Planning ▸ Fuel, not just Finance). Your AI can tell you exactly where to click.

November 9, 2026

Belly cargo: freight in the holds of your passenger flights (new games)

Games you start from today carry freight under the cabin floor. Games already in progress keep freight on freighters only, and nothing in them changes. You can switch it off on the setup screen.

  • Every passenger flight has a hold. What it can take is the smaller of the hold itself and the weight the aircraft has to spare at that distance. A 787-9 carries about 14 tonnes across the Atlantic and nothing at the very edge of its range; a narrow-body carries about a tonne.
  • It is a second income for long-haul. On a widebody route belly cargo adds roughly 4–9% to revenue and more than that to profit. On narrow-bodies it is small.
  • It is not free. Every tonne pays handling at both ends and the extra fuel burned carrying it, typically a fifth to a third of what it earns, and more when fuel is dear.
  • You set the rate, route by route. Each route’s detail page shows what its holds carried and earned, with the belly rate beside it. Leave it and it follows the market. The bulk pricing tools on the Routes page have a Belly cargo box too. See route economics.
  • Rivals do it too. Full-service rivals sell their hold space; budget carriers don’t.
  • Freighters share the lane. Holds and freighters draw on the same freight, so a lane full of passenger widebodies leaves less for a freighter. Outsize, hazardous and express freight still needs a main deck, so freighters always keep part of every lane, and the cargo hubs with few passenger flights are theirs.

November 9, 2026

Guides and in-game help brought back in line with the game

  • Delivery times read correctly. The Market screen and the in-game Wiki used to say a turboprop arrives in one week and a widebody in four. The first aircraft of a type has always taken twice that, and newer games deliver off shared production lines. Both now say so. See fleet planning.
  • One name for one number. A route’s profit after its share of the aircraft’s lease and maintenance was called “True profit” on some screens and “Fully-loaded profit” on others. It is Fully-loaded profit everywhere now, in the game and in the route economics guide and case study.
  • The Wiki covers newer games properly: how an era game ends in 2050, the smaller starting cash of an early historical start, all four cabins, and what flying the fleet hard really costs in punctuality under the 100-hour cap. See on-time performance.
  • Loan cards state the real limit: the headline amount or a multiple of your weekly revenue, whichever is higher.
  • Guide corrections. The aircraft count is 207 everywhere, the 787-9’s fuel burn in the fuel hedging guide matches the game, the demand & quality guide shows the frequency weights newer games use, and the case study’s block hours include taxi time. Every guide is now linked from the footer of every page.

November 8, 2026

Replace a whole type in one go

  • Retire a type without tagging aircraft one by one. Open any order in your order queue and use Replace a whole type: every aircraft of that type on order that isn’t already replacing something takes over one of the type you choose to retire. The soonest delivery goes to your oldest aircraft.
  • Same hand-over as before. Each new aircraft takes over the old one’s routes, frequencies and fares when it arrives, and the old one is sold, returned or kept as you chose. One click clears the whole plan again. See fleet planning.

November 6, 2026

See the cabin: floor plans, cabin painting and seat products

  • A floor plan of the real aircraft. The cabin refit screen now draws the aircraft from above with every seat on it, so you can see what a layout looks like before you pay for it.
  • Paint the cabins. Brush a cabin onto the rows you want, or drag the dividers between cabins.
  • Seat products for each cabin. Choose the pitch, lie-flat seats, suites, seat-back screens, a bar on wide-bodies and a shower on double-deckers. What you can fit depends on the year and on the airframe, and roomier products take more floor.
  • The right passengers notice. A better premium cabin lifts your appeal to business travellers; a better economy cabin lifts it with leisure travellers. See demand & quality.

November 6, 2026

Tail logos and custom tails

  • Design your tail. The logo maker has a new Tail section: five designs, your own tail and design colours, and your logo on the fin if you want it.
  • Or upload one. A tail image of your own is fitted to the fin shape and saved with your airline.
  • Your tail flies over your hubs on the Network map.

November 6, 2026

A clearer map, and where the money went

  • Line width by traffic. Switch on Width on the Network map and busier routes are drawn thicker, by last week’s passengers.
  • Colour by load factor. The map can now colour routes by how full they fly instead of by profit, in five bands from cool to hot. Both choices are remembered in your browser.
  • “Where the money went” on the Dashboard. A compact chart walks last week’s revenue down through flying, fleet, staff, gates and head office, brand, and loans and tax to net cash, and links through to Finance for the detail. You can show this week’s projection instead.
  • Week-on-week arrows on load factor, passengers, yield and fleet show which way each is heading.

November 6, 2026

The jet age, and the first 737s

  • Era games started from today: travellers want jets. Once the 707 and DC-8 are flying, passengers stop choosing propellers for longer trips. Between 1958 and 1965 a piston or turboprop airliner loses up to 35% of its demand on sectors over about 1,600 km, less on shorter ones, and nothing under 400 km, so props still own the short hops. Against a jet at the same fare a long-haul prop keeps about two in five travellers. A route's detail page shows the hit whenever it applies. Games already in progress keep the old rules.
  • The Boeing 737-100 joins the fleet (every game). Launched by Lufthansa in 1968, it is the shortest and rarest 737 — only 30 were built before airlines moved to the -200.
  • The 737-200 now arrives in 1968, when United first flew it, rather than 1971 (when the -200 Advanced took over the same line). See the narrow-body guide.

November 6, 2026

New games: frequency sells seats, a world economy, and a board that sets goals

Games you start from today run a newer set of rules. Games already in progress keep playing exactly as before.

  • How often you fly matters, even on a route you have to yourself. A daily service is the yardstick: twice a week reaches noticeably fewer travellers, several flights a day reach more (business travellers most of all). Against a rival, frequency wins more than its share — three times their flights takes around four in five business travellers. See route economics.
  • Superjumbos need superjumbo airports. The A380 and the 747-8I can only use the big international gateways with stands built for them, and the route planners only offer them there.
  • Big hubs are cheaper per gate, not dearer. Gate rent is a flat rate by airport size, with a discount once you hold more than ten gates at one airport.
  • A world economy. A business cycle a few years long now lifts and lowers demand everywhere, and moves the rate new leases are signed at. The Dashboard shows whether the economy is expanding, slowing, contracting or recovering. Lock cheap leases in the downturn. Demand events still happen, but less often and harder.
  • Run it flat-out and it can break. Fly your fleet past about 85% of its hours with no spare aircraft, or let crew morale slide, and a bad week can turn into an operational meltdown that costs satisfaction and reputation. A well-run airline carries no risk.
  • Board mandates. From your second quarter, the board sets one goal each quarter — grow traffic, widen the margin, fill the aircraft, please passengers, reach a new country or open new routes — worth a $1.5M bonus if you hit it in time.

For every game, old and new:

  • 787s and A350s now cruise faster and burn less fuel than before, in line with the real aircraft. See the wide-body guide.
  • Dakar has two airports. DKR is now Dakar’s original Léopold Sédar Senghor airport at its real site, instead of a second copy of Blaise Diagne (DSS).

November 5, 2026

Smoother with a big airline: faster pages, quieter in the background

  • The game sits still when you do. The “next week in…” countdown used to make the whole game redraw itself every second, whatever page you had open. Now only the countdown ticks, so a big Fleet or Finance page left open no longer keeps your computer busy.
  • The Market opens about twice as fast. Aircraft cards appear straight away and fill in as you look, and aircraft photos only load as you scroll to them.
  • Big fleets open without a stall. The Fleet page shows your first aircraft at once and the rest a moment later, instead of freezing while it builds hundreds of rows. Find-in-page still finds every aircraft.
  • The Competition page is quicker on big networks.
  • The game starts faster. Pages load the first time you open them instead of all at start-up, and the rest load quietly in the background while you look at your Dashboard.

November 5, 2026

Freighter conversions

Old passenger jets now have a second career. If you own an aircraft whose family has a freighter version, open it in Fleet and click Convert to freighter. It goes into the hangar and comes back as that freighter, ready for cargo routes.

  • 17 passenger types can convert, including the 737-800 (to the 737-800BCF), the A321ceo (to the A321P2F), the E190, the 767, the A330-200, the A300-600, the MD-11 and DC-10, the 747-400 and 747-200, the 757-200, the 727-200, the DC-8 and the Electra. See the freighter guide for what each one carries.
  • A conversion costs about 18% of the freighter’s price and takes 10 to 20 weeks, depending on the aircraft’s size. In production-line games it also needs a slot on the conversion line, so a busy line can add a wait. The confirmation shows the cost and when the aircraft will be back.
  • A converted aircraft runs like one 10 years younger. It stays its real age, but the conversion includes a heavy check, so its maintenance, repair bills and breakdown risk drop to those of a younger airframe, and its C and D check clocks reset. A 30-year-old A321 goes from 5.5× new-aircraft maintenance to 3×.
  • Its value doesn’t jump. The airframe keeps depreciating as the passenger aircraft it was built as, and the conversion is added on top and written off over 15 years.
  • You can convert several at once from the Fleet list: tick them and click Convert to freighter.
  • Only aircraft you own can be converted, so buy out a lease first. An aircraft still flying routes has to close them, and the confirmation offers to do that for you. Conversions are one-way.
  • Freighters no longer count toward your fleet’s age in reputation. Passengers judge the aircraft they fly on, so an old freighter fleet stops dragging your brand down. All-cargo airlines are scored on their whole fleet as before.
  • Maintenance figures on the Dashboard, Finance and Fleet screens now match what you’re actually charged, including the reduction from D checks.

Thanks to Barca and VodkaOnFire on Discord for the suggestion.

November 5, 2026

Route Finder presets

If you hunt for routes the same few ways, you no longer have to set the Route Finder up from scratch each time. Set up a search, click + Save this search and give it a name. It appears as a preset above the search, and one click brings it back.

  • A preset saves the whole search: the aircraft, the distance band, the region, the sort and the filter ticks, such as “No competitors only”. For example, an E195 on 0–1,500 km sorted by biggest market, or an A350-1000 on 13,000+ km sorted by best estimated profit with no competitors.
  • The origin isn’t saved, so a preset works from whichever airport you search from.
  • The preset you’re on is highlighted. Change any setting and the highlight goes. Saving under an existing name updates that preset, and × deletes one.
  • The Passenger and Freight finders each have their own presets, up to 12 each.
  • Presets are kept in your browser and carry over to every game you play in it. If a preset’s aircraft isn’t available yet, the rest of the preset still applies and the finder tells you.

Thanks to Barca on Discord for the suggestion.

November 5, 2026

Randomized worlds: preview, roll until, and share

Randomized passenger demand used to be a blind draw. You only saw a world after you launched it, and its number was gone once the game began. Now:

  • Preview a world before you launch. On the Launch step, Preview this world shows how your hub rolled, the biggest booms and slumps, and which airports changed tier. The preview follows the world number as you reroll. The hub list on the Home hub step shows every airport’s roll and tier in that world, so you can pick a hub that boomed, or one that slumped if you want a harder start.
  • Roll until you get the world you want. Roll until… takes up to five conditions, such as “DEN rolls at least +25%” or “AUS becomes a major airport”, and rolls worlds until one meets them all. It only searches the dice and never edits a world, so anything it finds could have come up by chance. Each airport shows the range it can roll, and a condition it can never meet is flagged before you start.
  • Your world number stays with the game. A randomized game shows its world number and mega setting at the top of the Airports page and in the map view’s Settings menu, with a Copy button.
  • Sharing is copy and paste. Copy gives a line like “Tailwinds world #123456 · megas capped”. Paste it into World # on the new-game screen and you get both the number and the mega setting.

New to hub choice? The hub strategy guide covers what makes a good home base.

Thanks to VodkaOnFire on Discord for the suggestion.

November 5, 2026

Freight now connects through your airports

Until now a freighter route only carried freight between its own two cities. Fly Hong Kong–Anchorage and Anchorage–Chicago and you got nothing from Hong Kong–Chicago freight, even though that is exactly how real freight networks work. Now:

  • Freight changes aircraft wherever two of your freighter routes meet. You don’t need to make the airport a hub, so an Anchorage-style transit stop works as well as your home base.
  • A route’s own freight loads first. Connecting freight only fills payload the route’s own freight leaves empty, so no route loses freight it already carries. A route with spare payload now has something to fill it with, which can make an extra frequency pay.
  • Only sensible routings. Freight won’t take a detour of more than about 30%, so Hong Kong–Tokyo freight never goes via Dubai, and the more direct the connection, the more of the market it wins.
  • It is contested. A nonstop freighter on the same market, whether yours or a rival’s, takes the bigger share. Pricing your legs above the going rate wins less connecting freight, just as it does on your routes’ own freight.
  • Revenue is split between the two flights by distance, and freight changing aircraft pays a handling charge at the connecting airport.
  • You can see it. Freight routes that carry connecting freight show a green “connecting” tag. Hover over it for the markets and where they connect. The freight summary shows how much of your freight revenue is connecting, and the freight Route Planner shows what a new route would pick up and what it adds to the routes it connects with.

This applies to games already in progress as well as new ones. More on building a network in the route economics guide.

Thanks to Barca on Discord for the suggestion.

November 5, 2026

Your Gates remembers how you sort it, on phones too

From a Discord request by VodkaOnFire: the gate list kept going back to region order with North America on top. The table view already remembered your sort; the card view you get on a phone didn’t have one.

  • The card view has a Sort picker with the same choices as the table: airport, region, gates, slots used, use, weekly cost and fuel. Tap the arrow next to it to reverse the order.
  • One sort for both views. Sort the table on your laptop and the cards come up in the same order, and the other way round.
  • The cards remember your region tab, and there is a new All tab that pages through every gate you hold, so a sort can run across your whole network.

All of this is remembered in your browser between visits and reloads. More on choosing where to lease gates in the route economics guide.

November 5, 2026

Aircraft fly up to 100 hours a week (new games)

Each aircraft could be scheduled for 140 block hours a week: 20 hours a day, every day. Real airlines don’t fly their aircraft that hard; a busy A321 or 737 manages 9 to 11 hours a day. In new games the limit is now 100 hours a week, the same as in Headwinds.

  • The 100-hour limit applies everywhere you schedule: opening routes, adding flights, multi-stop routes, freight lanes, charter contracts and moving routes between aircraft. The planners, the Fleet page and the utilisation bars all count against 100 hours.
  • Plan for more aircraft. A short, busy route that one aircraft used to cover may now need two. Fewer hours per aircraft also leaves more slack in the schedule, so flying a full fleet costs much less on-time performance than before.
  • Nothing already flying is cut. An aircraft scheduled for more than 100 hours, such as one that came with an airline you bought, keeps every flight it has. You just can’t add more to it until it is back under the limit, and lowering its frequency is always allowed.

New games only: existing saves keep the 140-hour limit. More on scheduling aircraft in the fleet planning guide.

November 5, 2026

Rivals stop to refuel, and chase the routes you gave them (new games)

In era games, AI airlines no longer give up on long routes the aircraft of the day can’t fly nonstop.

  • Refuelling stops. When nothing on the market can fly a route nonstop, a rival can fly it with one stop on the way, as airlines really did: Los Angeles–Tokyo via Honolulu in the 1950s, London–Sydney through the Gulf in the 1970s. Passengers stay on board, so only the end-to-end market is sold, and a stop costs the airline trip time against a nonstop and the expense of an extra landing.
  • They go nonstop when they can. Once an aircraft that reaches nonstop comes on the market, an airline flying through a stop re-equips, as long as it can afford the new aircraft and the nonstop earns more.
  • Stops follow the map of the day. Rivals refuel at real long-haul airports and keep out of airspace that was closed to them in that era.
  • Custom rival sets: listed routes become goals. A route you list for a rival that no aircraft of the era can reach, even with a stop, is no longer dropped for good. The airline opens it as soon as an aircraft can, ahead of anything else it was planning. If it later gives the route up after losing money, it waits a couple of years before trying again.
  • See it on the map. A rival route through a stop is drawn through it, and the stop is shown wherever you compare yourself with rivals on a route.
  • Taking one over. Buy a rival that flies through a stop and the route becomes one of your multi-stop routes, so the two shorter markets on the way are yours to sell as well.

This is part of new games only; existing saves keep their rivals as they were. More on how rivals behave in the competition guide.

November 5, 2026

Filters for fleet renewal

Picking which aircraft a new order replaces got a lot quicker on a big fleet.

  • Filter the aircraft you could replace. When you choose what an order replaces, from the order form or from an order already on the books, you can now search by name, tail or type, narrow to one type, show owned or leased only, and hide the aircraft that order can’t take over from.
  • Select everything you can see. On the order form, filter down to, say, your owned A320s and tick them all at once. Selections hidden by the filter stay selected.
  • Filter what’s on order. The On Order list on the Fleet page and the Orders tab in the market can be filtered by type, purchase or lease, and whether an order is already replacing an aircraft, so the ones still to be paired up are easy to find.

The filters show up once a list has five or more entries. More on renewing a fleet in the fleet planning guide.

November 4, 2026

Eight 1960s–70s freighters, and a more efficient A220

Era games used to jump from the An-12 (1959) straight to the DC-10-30F (1980), so a 1960s cargo airline had nothing to move up to for twenty years. These fill the gap, in order of entry into service:

  • Canadair CL-44D4 (1961): the swing-tail turboprop. 29 tonnes, cheap per tonne, slow.
  • Boeing 707-320C (1963): the first big jet freighter. 40 tonnes a long way, on a long runway.
  • Boeing 727-100C (1966): a small jet freighter for short sectors.
  • Douglas DC-8-63CF (1968): 50 tonnes, more than the 707, thirstier than the later -73F.
  • Lockheed L-188F Electra (1968): a converted Electra, 13 tonnes off short regional fields.
  • Lockheed L-100-30 Hercules (1970): 23 tonnes into strips nothing else can use.
  • Boeing 747-200F (1972): the first 100-tonne freighter, with a nose that swings open.
  • Ilyushin Il-76T (1979): the An-12’s jet successor, at home on rough runways.

In era games each one sells new while its real production line was open and second-hand after. They’re in every game, including existing saves. More in the freighter guide.

The A220-300 now burns about 3% less fuel than the A319neo, as it does in real life (281 L per 100 km, down from 321). The A220-100 drops to 266 L so it still burns less than the bigger -300.

Freighters requested by The Dragon Overlord and read2much. on Discord. Added to Headwinds as well.
